title: Nichiren
hookLine: the monk who taught chanting the Lotus Sutra's title, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo

lines: A MONK WHO PICKED A TITLE.
cards: In homes and community centers, people kneel or sit before a scroll and chant one phrase, steadily, again and again, a rolling rhythm that can fill a room: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo.

No long instructions to memorize, no complicated posture. Just a phrase, a voice and a scroll. That chant goes back to a Japanese monk who said the title of one sutra held the whole of the Buddha's teaching.

teach.b: Nichiren was a monk in Japan who studied widely and came to one conviction: the Lotus Sutra was the Buddha's highest teaching, and the way into it was its title.
Tradition says he first chanted the phrase aloud at his home temple, facing the sunrise. Open the phrase. Namu means something like devotion, or I take refuge in.
Myoho is the wonderful law, or mystic law, the truth the sutra teaches. Renge is the lotus, which grows out of mud and blooms clean. Kyo is sutra, a teaching.
Myoho Renge Kyo is the sutra's title; namu is the devotion placed in front of it. Together: devotion to the Lotus Sutra of the wonderful law. Why a title?
In Nichiren's teaching, the title isn't a label on the outside of a book.

It holds the whole sutra, the way a seed holds a tree. So chanting it meets the entire teaching with your own voice, not only your eyes or your intellect, which opens the practice to anyone, not just scholar monks.
Nichiren was outspoken. He wrote that Japan's troubles came from turning away from the Lotus, he argued hard with the schools of his day, and tradition remembers that he was sent into exile for it.
Today his followers belong to several groups, including Nichiren Shu, Nichiren Shoshu and Soka Gakkai, which differ on how to read his teaching and who carries it forward.
What they share is the chant. For Nichiren Buddhists, saying the title isn't a warm-up for practice. It is the practice.

how: Nichiren Buddhists chant Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, called the daimoku, often morning and evening before a scroll called the Gohonzon, and recite passages from the Lotus Sutra; groups meet in homes and temples to chant together.

games.q: you're Nichiren. which part of the Lotus Sutra do you teach people to chant, as holding the whole teaching?
games.why: Nichiren taught chanting namu, devotion, before the title, Myoho Renge Kyo, which holds the sutra like a seed holds the tree.

practice: If you'd like, chant the title three times at an easy, steady pace, the way Nichiren Buddhists do: Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo, Namu Myoho Renge Kyo. If saying it isn't right for you, simply hear it in your head.
Then let it go quiet, and feel what the sound leaves behind in the chest, the throat, the room.

carryVoice: Your line: the title of the Lotus. A whole teaching, held in a name. A thousand days on the path, and still walking.
